title: Numerical Methods & Statistical Evidence
description: Study stable log-sum-exp, finite differences and gradient checks, bootstrap uncertainty and dependence, and multiple comparisons and effect sizes. Each lesson includes a worked example and an applied practice task.

lessons.title: Stable log-sum-exp
lessons.description: Write the stabilized expression and explain why the result is unchanged.
lessons.conceptOverview: Compute log-sum-exp by subtracting the largest input before exponentiation and adding it back afterward. This preserves the mathematical value while reducing overflow risk.
lessons.whyItMatters: Algebraically equivalent computations can differ greatly in numerical stability.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Directly exponentiating logits 1000 and 1001 can overflow, while subtracting 1001 yields exponentials of negative one and zero.

lessons.title: Finite differences and gradient checks
lessons.description: Sweep several step sizes and inspect relative and absolute error.
lessons.conceptOverview: Central finite differences approximate a derivative using nearby evaluations. Too large a step adds truncation error; too small a step amplifies floating-point cancellation. Compare with tolerances and avoid nondifferentiable points.
lessons.whyItMatters: Gradient checks need a suitable perturbation scale.

lessons.title: Bootstrap uncertainty and dependence
lessons.description: Design a user-level bootstrap and compare its interpretation.
lessons.conceptOverview: Bootstrap estimates variability by resampling according to assumptions about the data. Independent row resampling is inappropriate when observations are strongly grouped or sequential; use a scheme that respects dependence.
lessons.whyItMatters: Resampling should preserve the relevant dependence structure.

lessons.title: Multiple comparisons and effect sizes
lessons.description: Describe a correction or validation strategy and report the search process.
lessons.conceptOverview: Trying many hypotheses increases the chance of apparently significant findings. Report effect sizes, uncertainty and the selection process; distinguish exploratory analysis from a preplanned test.
